title: A Space Telescope Opens Its Eyes After Eight Years
summary: After eight years in space, a telescope built in the UK has opened its eyes. Called MIXS, it is travelling to Mercury on the BepiColombo mission after a journey of 10 billion kilometres. Its first target was the Crab Nebula, the leftover cloud of an exploded star about 6,500 light-years away. The nebula gives off a strong, steady X-ray signal, so it was a perfect test target. Scientists at the University of Leicester are checking MIXS as BepiColombo prepares to enter orbit around Mercury on November 21. The main test took place on September 11 and 12, and over 39 hours the spacecraft turned 55 times to collect data. The results are better than expected: MIXS sees fine details more sharply than in lab tests on Earth in 2015, with no radiation damage to its detector. Professor Emma Bunce called the results fantastic and noted that 80 percent of the technology on MIXS is new. The team will fine-tune MIXS at Mercury, where it will study what the surface is made of and how planets form close to a star.
why_it_matters: Learning how planets form helps us understand how Earth and our own solar system came to be.

background_read: MIXS is a telescope on the BepiColombo spacecraft, which is travelling to Mercury, the planet closest to the Sun.
A telescope in space can study light, like X-rays, that our eyes cannot see, and scientists use it to learn what planets are made of and how they form.
Before reaching Mercury, the team tested MIXS by pointing it at the Crab Nebula, a steady and bright target left over from an exploded star.
